content.text:
Pick up issue #113 in super-star-trek: sst.doc documents -t and its 72x24 minimum around lines 1544-1547 but says nothing    
  about resizing. All of that behaviour is only in README.md, and sst.doc is the manual reached from inside the game — so the  
  players most likely to drag a window can't see it.                                                                           
                                                                                                                               
  Follow the workflow in AGENTS.md, including checking the issue's premises before building on them.                           
                                                                                                                               
  Three things worth knowing up front:                                                                                         
                                                                                                                               
  1. sst.doc is CRLF and the game reads it at runtime. Under curses a trailing \r returns the cursor to column 0 and the       
  newline erases the line. sst.c:662 strips it. Verify new text through the in-game help, not just in an editor.               
  2. ui-review binds — this is text the game prints, not an instruction file.                                                  
  3. The content already exists and is reviewed. README.md's resize paragraphs went through several review rounds and are      
  accurate as of commit fef362c. The manual wants the player-facing consequences, not the reasoning about why the conversation 
  can't be rebuilt — don't copy them wholesale.                                                                                
                                                                                                                               
  Two specifics that took real work to establish, so don't re-derive or contradict them: the line you're on usually comes back 
  on a resize, but a question you'd already started answering does not (that's #117). At that one, tell the player to press    
  Ctrl-U before answering — a yes/no prompt reads the first letter, so an unseen y in the buffer makes a typed N mean yes, and 
  that can end the game.                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                               
  When you run the TUI test suite, run it as sh tests/tui.sh ./build/sst Debug. Without that second argument the sensors block 
  is silently skipped.
I'll start by inspecting the repo state and the issue.

state:	OPEN

--
`sst.doc` documents the `-t` option and its 72x24 minimum at lines 1544-1547, but
says nothing about what happens when the terminal is resized while the game is
running. All of that behaviour is documented only in `README.md`.

## Why it matters

`sst.doc` is what a player reaches from inside the game — it is the manual the
game itself points at. `README.md` is what someone reads on the repository page
before they have played. So the audience most likely to resize a window mid-game
is the one that cannot see any of this.

What is missing from the manual, all of it currently true and all of it in
`README.md`:

- resizing is safe at any point, including while the game waits for an answer
  or for a keystroke at a pause
- below 72x24 the panels clip rather than rearrange, and a clipped line ends in
  `>` so a shortened number is not mistaken for a small one
- growing back brings the panels with it however far the squeeze went, but the
  conversation that scrolled away is gone
- the line you are on usually comes back whole; a few prompts do not, and Enter
  re-prompts

## Scope

Pre-existing and untouched by the fix for #100, which is where it was noticed.

## Fix sketch

A short paragraph in the manual's `-t` section. It should not duplicate
`README.md` wholesale — the manual wants the player-facing consequences, not the
reasoning about why the conversation cannot be rebuilt.

Note that `sst.doc` is CRLF and is read by the game at runtime, so anything
added there is subject to the trailing-carriage-return rule in `AGENTS.md`.

## Provenance

Found by the `ui-review` sub-agent while reviewing #100's fix. Filed rather than
fixed there, per AGENTS.md step 9.

# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
A terminal shorter than the panels themselves loses rows off the bottom
of them, the grid keeping its numbering so you can see where it stops.

Shorter than fourteen rows there is no room left for the conversation
at all: the panels are the whole screen and the prompt is not on it.
Just above that there is barely more — at fourteen rows the one line
left over goes entirely to the pager, so a scan pages past without
showing any of itself; at fifteen it comes one line at a time.

Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.

The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
row.
Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
lines returns as the last of them. The one gap left is a question you
have already started answering: that one is left exactly as it was
before, so what comes back may be a stump of older conversation, or
nothing, with the game still waiting behind it.

Do not just answer that one, and do not press Enter either: whatever
you typed is still in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the
*first* letter, so an `N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.

Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
typed stay where they landed.

If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
prompt, free to give the command again.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead.

The build is CMake, and a build type is required:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   # or Release
cmake --build build
./build/sst
```

#112 restores a prompt that ended its own line — `prout` appends the newline, so
`curline` is empty by the time the reader waits, and the question used to vanish
on a resize. The fix keeps the finished line and puts it back.

It deliberately does **not** do so once the player has begun typing.

## Why

An ended prompt and its part-typed answer occupy two rows, with curses' padding
between them. `restore_curline()` compares against a single joined string, and
spanning that boundary went wrong twice in review:

- Leaving the answer out of the comparison meant the tail test never fired, so a
  drag reprinted the question **once per width step** — copies stacking up the
  window, which is the exact failure `restore_curline()`'s comparison exists to
  prevent.
- Padding the answer back to the row boundary fixed that and turned a one-row
  height shrink (80x24 → 80x23) into a **second copy** instead.

Both were found by `ui-review`; the second was my fix for the first.

## What happens now

With an answer part typed, an ended prompt is left alone on a resize — the
behaviour before #112. The answer itself is still restored by the ordinary
`curline` path, so the player can see what they have typed; the question above
it is at worst truncated, exactly as it was.

That is milder than either failure above, which is why it is the state that
ships. It is still worth fixing.

## Fix sketch

The comparison needs to model two rows rather than one. Either:

1	#!/bin/sh
2	# Covers the game's handling of sst.doc, which has CRLF line endings.
3	#
4	# The manual is read from that file and printed like any other game
5	# text, so a trailing carriage return travels with it. In the plain
6	# display that is invisible; under curses the CR sends the cursor back
7	# to column 0 and the newline then erases the line, which once left
8	# `help` printing nothing at all. The same applies to input: a script
9	# written on Windows arrives with carriage returns attached to every
10	# command.
11	#
12	# Every case here ends the game by running out of input, so the pager
13	# never steals a character from a command still to come. Each plays in
14	# a directory of its own holding the sst.doc that case needs, since
15	# `help` reads it from the current directory.
16	#
17	# Usage: help.sh /path/to/sst
18	
19	set -u
20	
21	SST="${1:-./sst}"
22	# The cases below run from directories of their own.
23	case "$SST" in
24		/*) ;;
25		*) SST="$(pwd)/$SST" ;;
26	esac
27	srcdir=$(unset CDPATH; cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
28	
29	CR=$(printf '\r')	# BSD sed reads a regex \r as a literal r
30	MAXBYTES=262144
31	DUMPBYTES=2048

cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/add.txt" <<'EOF'

  Resizing the terminal is safe at any point, including while the
  game waits for an answer or for a keystroke at a pause. Dragged
  below 72x24 the panels clip rather than rearrange: a line with
  more to show than there is room for ends in ">", so a shortened
  number is never mistaken for a small one. Growing the terminal
  back brings the panels with it however far the squeeze went, since
  they redraw from the game state; the conversation that scrolled
  away does not come back, but no reading is lost with it, and
  srscan, status, chart and damages all cost nothing.

  The line you are on usually returns with the panels, so a resize
  does not leave you typing into the tail of a question. If a prompt
  is missing or cut short and you have not begun answering, press
  Enter; nothing that waits behind one commits you to anything. If
  you had begun, the question is not put back: press Ctrl-U before
  you answer, because what you typed is still in the line unseen,
  and a yes/no question reads only its first letter -- an "N" typed
  after a "y" you cannot see answers yes, and some of those
  questions can end the game.
EOF
awk 'BEGIN{RS="\n"} {printf "%s\r\n", $0}' "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/add.txt" | head -c -0 > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/add.crlf"
# drop the trailing empty record awk adds
python3 - <<'PY'
import os
p = os.environ['CLAUDE_JOB_DIR'] + '/tmp/add.txt'
with open(p, 'rb') as f:
    body = f.read()
if body.endswith(b'\n'):
    body = body[:-1]
crlf = body.replace(b'\n', b'\r\n') + b'\r\n'
doc = open('sst.doc','rb').read()
lines = doc.split(b'\r\n')
# line 1549 is index 1548 ("  classic display rather than failing.")
assert lines[1548] == b'  classic display rather than failing.', lines[1548]
out = b'\r\n'.join(lines[:1549]) + b'\r\n' + crlf + b'\r\n'.join(lines[1549:])
open('sst.doc','wb').write(out)
print("inserted")
PY

input.command:
cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/issue.md" <<'EOF'
`helpme()` (`sst.c:127-199`) is the only thing that opens `sst.doc`, and it
prints exactly one shape of entry. It builds a key of `  Mnemonic:  <COMMAND>`
— or ` ABBREV` for the abbreviation table — scans forward for the first line
carrying that prefix, and prints until a line containing `******`.

So the only text `help` can reach is a command entry. The last one is
`  Mnemonic:  SCORE` at `sst.doc:1294`, and the `ABBREV` table is at
`sst.doc:1406`. Everything after that is unreachable from inside the game:

- `MISCELLANEOUS NOTES` (1302) — black holes, the Neutral Zone, ramming
  commanders, how fast the Super-commander travels
- `SCORING` (1349) — the whole scoring table
- `MODIFICATIONS` (1471), which includes the full-screen `-t` section at
  1541 and everything #113 is adding to it
- `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS` (1552) and `REFERENCES` (1573)

## Why it matters

The game names `sst.doc` to the player and refuses to give help without it
("You need to find SST.DOC and put it in the current directory", `sst.c:163`),
which reads as a promise that the file is the manual the game will show you.
It shows you a fifth of it. A player who wants to know what the scoring
actually is, or what happens when they drag the window, has to leave the game
and open the file in a pager.

This is what makes #113's premise only half true — the manual is the right
home for that text, but adding it there does not put it in front of a player
mid-game.

## How to see it

```sh
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug && cmake --build build
printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nhelp score\n' | ./build/sst
```

`help score` prints the `SCORE` *command* entry (`sst.doc:1294`), not the
`SCORING` section (1349). There is no argument at all that reaches 1541.

## Fix sketch

`help` would need a way to name a topic that is not a command. Either a
second key shape in `helpme()` — a `  Topic:  <NAME>` line placed above the
narrative sections, terminated the same way — or a `help display` /
`help scoring` special-cased the way ` ABBREV` already is at `sst.c:152-154`.
Whichever it is, `listCommands()` and the `HELP` entry in `sst.doc` would
have to say the topics exist, or nobody will guess them.

## Provenance

Found while doing #113, checking the claim that `sst.doc` is what a player
reaches from inside the game. Filed rather than fixed there, per AGENTS.md
step 9.
EOF
gh issue create --title "Most of sst.doc is unreachable from in-game help" --body-file "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/issue.md"

input.command:
cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/comment.md" <<'EOF'
Checked this issue's premises before building on them. Three corrections;
none of them changes the fix sketch, but one of them changes what the
paragraph has to say.

**The `-t` section is at `sst.doc:1541-1549`, not 1544-1547.** Line 1544 does
carry the 72x24 minimum, but 1541-1545 are the paragraph introducing the
option and 1547-1549 are the fallback notice. The new text goes after 1549.

**"`sst.doc` is what a player reaches from inside the game" does not hold for
this section.** `helpme()` (`sst.c:127-199`) is the only thing that opens the
file, and it prints one shape of entry: it builds `  Mnemonic:  <COMMAND>`
(or ` ABBREV`), scans for the first line with that prefix, and prints until a
line containing `******`. The last such entry is `  Mnemonic:  SCORE` at
`sst.doc:1294`; the `ABBREV` table is at 1406. Everything after that —
`MISCELLANEOUS NOTES`, `SCORING`, `MODIFICATIONS` (where the `-t` section
lives), `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS`, `REFERENCES` — is never printed by the game. A
player reaches this text by opening the file, not with `help`.

That narrows the "Why it matters" argument rather than voiding it. `sst.doc`
still ships with the game, still has to sit in the working directory for
`help` to work at all, and is still where a player looks rather than at a
repository page — so the manual remains the right home for this, and the fix
sketch stands as written. The reachability gap itself is now #120.

**"the line you are on usually comes back whole; a few prompts do not, and
Enter re-prompts" conflates two cases, and for one of them the advice is
dangerous.** What is actually true:

- *Prompt missing or cut short, nothing typed yet.* Enter is safe. A pause
  moves on, the self-destruct password reads an empty answer as a refusal,
  and a yes/no question comes back as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`.
- *An answer already part typed.* The question is not put back at all (#117),
  and Enter is exactly the wrong key. `ja()` (`sst.c:731-740`) takes the
  first token of the line and tests `*citem == 'y'`, so a `y` still sitting
  unseen in `tui_readline()`'s buffer makes a typed `N` answer yes — "yN"
  lowercases to "yn" and returns TRUE. The player has to press Ctrl-U
  (`tui.c:920`) first. Some of those questions cost the game: `events.c:420`
  asks "Are you sure?" before resting past your remaining time, or with
  enemies in the quadrant.

The paragraph as written tells the player to press Ctrl-U in the second case,
and keeps Enter for the first, where it is safe.
EOF
gh issue comment 113 --body-file "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/comment.md"

`sst.doc` is paginated with form feeds, and each page carries its number in
the heading line that follows the break. Measured between form feeds, the
pages run 47 to 67 lines — except `MODIFICATIONS` (page 26, `sst.doc:1471`),
which was already 81 lines and is 118 after the change for #113.

## Why it matters

Anyone printing or paging the manual gets one physical sheet per form feed.
Page 26 is now close to two of them, so the number printed at the top stops
agreeing with the sheet you are holding, and the page numbers in the table of
contents (`sst.doc:54-77`) stop being a way to find anything after it.

It is also a trap for the next person adding to the `-t` documentation, which
is where the growth is coming from: the section has no natural stopping point
and nothing signals that it has outgrown its page.

## How to see it

```sh
awk '/\f/{if (prev) printf "%d lines before the break at %d\n", NR-prev, NR; prev=NR}' sst.doc
```

The last three figures are 55, 67 and 118. Every other page in the file is
inside the 47-67 band.

## Fix sketch

Split `MODIFICATIONS` across two pages with a form feed and a `26 (cont.)`
style heading, or renumber from 26 onward — the latter also touches the table
of contents, since `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS` and `REFERENCES` follow. Renumbering is
the tidier result and the larger diff.

Worth deciding first whether the pagination is load-bearing at all: nothing in
the game reads it (`helpme()` skips form feeds outright, `sst.c:180`), and its
last help topic is at `sst.doc:1294`, well before this page. If the answer is
that nobody prints the manual, the honest fix may be to say so and stop
maintaining the numbers.

## Provenance

Found by `ui-review` while reviewing #113, as a nit against a change that
makes it worse without causing it. Filed rather than fixed there, per
AGENTS.md step 9.

<result>## Verdict

Needs changes — but small, textual ones. The change is documentation-only, so nothing in the running game regressed, and the paragraph's *advice* (look before you type; Ctrl-U; Enter is safe; answer N) is correct and I confirmed every step of it against a live `-t` session. Three of the five rewrites, however, now state things the game does not do: the "said only once" example is recoverable via `CHART`, the ended-own-line prompt claim contradicts the fix that this branch is built on (`fef362c`, #119), and the new width/height split got the height thresholds in the wrong order. All three are one-sentence fixes.

## Findings

### 1. should-fix — the starbase locations are *not* lost (`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.doc`, new paragraph 2)

> "-- but anything the game says only once is gone, the starbase locations in the opening briefing among them."

The star chart knows every starbase quadrant from setup: `setup.c:339` sets `starch[ix][iy] = -1` as each base is placed, and `reports.c:234` renders that as `.1.`. A player who loses the briefing to a resize gets the locations back with `CHART` — the very command the same sentence has just called free. Verified in plain mode: briefing listed `1 - 6  5 - 3  5 - 1  1 - 1`, and `CHART` at the first `COMMAND>` showed `.1.` at exactly those four cells.

This is the most actionable error in the change: it tells the player a one-off loss is unrecoverable when it is one free command away, and it is self-contradictory two clauses after listing `CHART`.

Suggestion: keep the rule, replace the example with something genuinely unrepeatable — the blow-by-blow of a fight ("what a torpedo did, or how hard you were just hit"), rather than anything the chart or `STATUS` re-derives. If a named example is wanted, check it against `starch`/`STATUS` first; several obvious candidates (Klingons remaining, supernovae, bases) are all recoverable.

### 2. should-fix — ended-own-line prompts *do* come back now (new paragraph 3)

> "A question that had finished its own line before stopping to wait is left as it was..."

That was true before `fef362c` and is what #119 fixed: `note_out()` now keeps the finished line in `lastline` and `restore_curline()` reprints it (`tui.c:423-441`). The surviving gap is narrower — `tui.c:436` returns only when `pending_answer` is non-empty, i.e. **once you have begun typing an answer** — which is issue #117, whose title says exactly that. The rewrite fixed finding 1 by dropping the "begun answering" condition and re-attached it to the wrong half.

Verified live at 80x24: `rest 5000` → `Are you sure?` (an ended line, `events.c:420`), shrink to 80x20 → the question was reprinted at the bottom. Typing `y` first and shrinking to 80x18 → question and `y` both gone, reader still waiting, bottom of screen showing an old long-range scan.

Suggestion: `"A question you had already begun answering may not come back at all, and what you are then looking at may be older conversation that reads exactly like a live prompt."` The following sentences need no change.

### 3. should-fix — the height thresholds are in the wrong order (new paragraph 1)

> "...only a terminal shorter than the panels themselves costs them rows off the bottom... **Shorter still** there is no room for conversation at all..."

Measured (`PANELH` is 13, `tui.c:15`; `msgh` at `tui.c:202`):

- 14 rows — one conversation line left
- 13 rows — no conversation at all, panels are the whole screen and complete
- 12 rows — panels lose their tenth scan row
- 11 rows — ninth row goes too

So the conversation runs out *first*, at 13 rows, and panel clipping begins *below* that. "Shorter still" inverts the sequence, and a player following the text would expect a clipped scan while a prompt is still visible — which never happens.

Suggestion: `"Shorter, it is the conversation that loses lines first, until at thirteen rows there is no room for it at all: the panels are the whole screen with no prompt on it. Shorter still and the panels lose rows off the bottom, the scan keeping its numbering so you can see where it stops. Nothing has gone wrong: grow the terminal back and both return."`

### 4. nit — the fourteen-row pager trap is unmentioned

`tui_pageheight()` is `LINES-PANELH-1` (`tui.c:987`), so at 14 rows it is 0. Verified at 80x14: `chart` printed nothing but `[HIT SPACE BAR TO CONTINUE]`, again and again, with no chart on screen. README documents this ("a scan pages past without showing any of itself"); the manual's "the conversation loses lines first" gives no hint of it, and to a player it reads as a hang rather than as a too-small window. One clause in the same sentence as the thresholds would cover it.

### 5. nit — the thresholds are only ever relative

"shorter than the panels themselves" is unactionable: nothing tells the player the panels are thirteen rows, and the section's only number is `72x24`. Naming the row counts (as README does) makes the paragraph checkable.

### 6. nit — "answer N there and give the command over" over-generalizes

At the post-game `Do you want to play again?` (`sst.c:507-508`) `N` ends the session, and there is no command to give over; and if the invisible reader is not a yes/no at all (a course, a number of units, the self-destruct password at `finish.c:25`) there is nothing to answer `N` to — Enter is still safe there, but the advice stops applying. Consider scoping it: "if what comes back is that re-ask, `N` declines whatever was asked and you can give the command again." Worth adding, too, that after Ctrl-U the player may simply type the answer they meant, once the re-ask has told them which question is waiting.

### 7. nit — punctuation of the quoted re-ask

`only as Please answer with "Y" or "N":, never repeating the question` puts a comma straight after the prompt's own colon. The manual quotes game text elsewhere with surrounding double quotes; quoting the whole prompt, or dropping its trailing colon, reads better in a plain-text file.

- "safe at any point, including while the game waits for an answer or for a keystroke at a pause" — `tui_readline`/`tui_getch` both handle `KEY_RESIZE` between reads (`tui.c:860`, `tui.c:960`).

- "some of those questions can end the game" — the deathray confirmation (`planets.c:420`) and the quit/play-again path qualify.
- Formatting: CRLF preserved, 2-space indent, longest new line 68 columns, blank-line spacing before `----------ACKNOWLEDGMENTS----------` unchanged.

cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/c117.md" <<'EOF'
While documenting this for #113 I checked the "What happens now" section
against the code, and one sentence in it is too kind:

> The answer itself is still restored by the ordinary `curline` path, so the
> player can see what they have typed; the question above it is at worst
> truncated, exactly as it was.

Neither half holds. `tui_readline()` echoes each typed character straight to
the window with `waddch(wmsg, c)` (`tui.c:938`) and never routes it through
`note_out()`, so a part-typed answer never reaches `curline` — `curlen` is
still 0 when the reader waits. `restore_curline()` therefore takes its
`curlen == 0` branch, hits the `pending_answer` gate at `tui.c:436`, and
returns having restored nothing. The re-echo at `tui.c:884` is gated on
`cursor_at_prompt`, which that early return leaves `FALSE`.

So with an ended prompt and a part-typed answer, a resize loses **both** the
question and the answer, and what is left at the bottom of the window is
whatever older conversation the squeeze brought into view.

Confirmed live by `ui-review` at 80x24: `rest 5000` → `Are you sure?`
(`events.c:420`, an ended line), type `y`, shrink to 80x18 — question and
answer both gone, reader still waiting, an old long-range scan sitting where
the prompt should be.

That makes the gap worse than the issue states, though not worse than the two
failures it was chosen over. It also raises the stakes on the recovery advice:
because nothing is restored, the player cannot tell from the screen that a
reader is waiting at all, which is why the manual paragraph added in #113
tells them to press Ctrl-U before answering anything after a resize.
EOF

The message window's depth is derived from two constants:

- `PANELH` is 13 (`tui.c:15`)
- `msgh = LINES-PANELH > 1 ? LINES-PANELH : 1` (`tui.c:202`)
- `tui_pageheight() = LINES-PANELH-1` (`tui.c:987`)

Which gives a three-step progression as the terminal gets shorter:

- **fifteen rows** — two message rows, one of which is the pager, so output
  arrives a line at a time
- **fourteen rows** — one message row, and `tui_pageheight()` is 0, so the
  pager takes the only line there is and a scan pages past without showing
  any of itself (this is the state #95 is about)
- **thirteen rows** — the message window starts at row `PANELH`, which is off
  a thirteen-row screen, so there is no conversation and no prompt anywhere
  (this is #94)
- **shorter** — `panelh = LINES` and the panels themselves start losing rows
  off the bottom

`tests/tui.sh` visits fourteen and eleven rows (`tests/tui.sh:1079`, `:1391`,
`:1507-1524`) but asserts panel geometry and prompt survival there, not this
progression. Nothing ties the numbers to the behaviour.

## Why it matters

`sst.doc` now states all three thresholds by name, as of the change for #113 —
"at fifteen rows it arrives a line at a time, at fourteen the pager takes the
only line there is and a scan pages past without showing any of itself, and at
thirteen there is none of it left at all". Those are the numbers a player uses
to decide whether the window they are looking at is broken or merely small.

Change `PANELH`, or the `-1` in `tui_pageheight()`, or the `> 1` guard on
`msgh`, and every one of those sentences becomes wrong while the whole suite
stays green. The manual is currently the only thing in the repository that
records the progression, and it is the one thing nothing checks.

```sh

```

content.text:
Merged. `main` is at `2f7f06d`, #113 is closed, branch deleted.

## What shipped

Four paragraphs in `sst.doc`'s `-t` section (46 lines, CRLF), covering what the manual never said about resizing a running game: that a resize never crashes the game or drops it back to the classic display; how the display gives way — panel lines clipping with a `>` marker below 72 columns, the conversation running out at fifteen, fourteen and thirteen rows *before* the panels lose rows of their own; what growing back restores and what it can't; and what to do at a prompt a resize has swallowed — press Ctrl-U before answering, because `ja()` reads the first letter of the first word and an `N` typed after an unseen `y` answers yes.

## Two things you should know

**The issue's central premise was wrong, and I built anyway.** `sst.doc` is *not* reachable from inside the game for this section — `helpme()` prints only per-command entries keyed by `  Mnemonic:  <COMMAND>` / ` ABBREV`, and the last one terminates 79 lines above the insertion point. So your instruction to "verify new text through the in-game help" couldn't be followed directly. I verified rendering by splicing the paragraphs into a real `SRSCAN` help entry in a scratch copy of the tree, building fresh there, and paging under curses at 72x24 and 80x24. The manual is still the right home (it ships with the binary and must sit in the working directory for `help` to work at all), so the slice stood — corrected on #113 by comment, gap filed as #120.

**`ui-review` took six rounds**, and rounds 1–2 found eight substantive errors, not style. The ones worth naming: the starbase locations were *not* an unrecoverable loss (`CHART` has them from setup, `setup.c:339`), the height thresholds were inverted, and the `>` marker is width-only. Rounds 3–6 came back clean; I cut off round 6 explicitly after three consecutive "acceptable as-is" verdicts were producing nits about the previous round's own wording.

## Issues filed

| | |
|---|---|
| #120 | Most of `sst.doc` is unreachable from in-game `help` |
| #121 | `MODIFICATIONS` has outgrown its page number (125 lines vs a 47–67 band; 81 before this) |
| #122 | README's resize section over-promises, then contradicts itself |
| #123 | Nothing ties the 15/14/13-row thresholds to their behaviour (verifier's finding) |

Plus a comment on **#117** correcting its body: with an ended prompt and a part-typed answer, a resize loses *both* the question and the answer — `tui_readline()` echoes with `waddch` and never calls `note_out()`, so `restore_curline()` returns at `tui.c:436` having restored nothing.

**No test was added** — the text is prose in a region no command can print, proved rather than assumed (the verifier diffed all 38 `help` outputs across the change and found them byte-identical). Six resolved-not-fixed findings are recorded in the PR body. On your note about test scope: the main agent ran only the two compiled unit tests (`tuifmt`, `rules`); the full battery ran in the `verifier`, and CI passed all four jobs.

Thinking through our main agent vs sub agent verifier. I want to keep the main agent context as clean as possible. We are
  doing tdd so we have to build and run tests. We also are doing user journey testing. How should we handle this? have the
  main agent run the one and the verifier run the entire suite?

Yes — that split is right. But I'd draw the line somewhere sharper than unit-vs-journey.

## The boundary that actually works

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The verifier runs everything else.**

Not "unit tests in main, journeys in the verifier" — that breaks the moment the focused test *is* a journey. If I'm changing the pager, `tests/tui.sh` is my red-green loop; delegating it means waiting minutes per iteration for a summary of the one observation TDD exists to produce. Conversely, if I'm changing `tuifmt.c`, the golden recordings aren't my focused test even though they're cheap-ish — they're regression surface, and that's the verifier's job.

The TDD inner loop can't be delegated at all. AGENTS.md step 4 wants you to *watch* the test fail for the expected reason; a sub-agent reporting "it failed correctly" is exactly the trust you're not supposed to extend.

| | Main agent | Verifier |
|---|---|---|
| Build (`--build build`) | ✅ ~5 lines | ✅ also, Release + `SST_WERROR` |
| The focused test, whatever it is | ✅ | — |
| Rest of `ctest` | — | ✅ |
| Full journey / golden / tournament | — | ✅ |
| Cross-config, cross-platform | — | ✅ (+ CI) |

## What actually cost context this session

Worth measuring before tuning. My own test running was nearly free — the unit tests were 8 lines and 0.01s; the build was 5 lines. Two things were expensive:

**tmux pane captures.** ~10 of them at 11–24 lines each. This is the one to fix in the main agent, and it's mechanical: grep the pane for the string you're asserting instead of dumping it. Capture the whole pane only when the grep fails. Same for `ctest` — `--output-on-failure` already prints nothing on success; `2>&1 | tail -5` on the shell scripts does the rest.

**Sub-agent reports, by a wide margin.** Six `ui-review` rounds at 60–100 lines each dwarfed everything I ran locally. That's the real lever on your stated goal. The "What I exercised" appendices were genuinely useful for auditing here — but if you want them shorter, that's a one-line change to the agent definitions, not to the test split.

## One more delegation worth making

The step-4 mutation proof — copy the tree, break the game, confirm the test catches it — is a good sub-agent candidate that isn't currently one. It's verbose (a full out-of-tree configure and build), it's one-shot rather than iterative, and its result is a single yes/no. The main agent still writes the comment beside the assertion, so it needs the sub-agent to report precisely *what* was broken.

Want me to write this into AGENTS.md as a step-4/step-7 clarification? It's the kind of rule that evaporates when the session ends otherwise — and it belongs next to the verifier's existing "scope appropriate for the change" language, which currently says nothing about who runs what.

# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
MINAGENTS=2000

fails=0
fail() {
	printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
	fails=$((fails + 1))
}

if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
fi
if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
fi
if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')

# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
fi
if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '## Development workflow' section -- the workflow every agent follows should live there"
fi

# Steps 6, 7 and 8 hold their review passes to one standard, and say it
# -- and not a coordinated edit that reworded a step and added the
# phrase somewhere else to keep the total at four. Issue #65 is where
# that check would live -- as filed it checks numbering, not which step
# a match fell in; the comment thread there asks for the attribution it
# would need.
#
# Counted over the file with its line breaks flattened, because the
# phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four places it appears: a
# check a rewrap can break is a check that gets deleted the first time
# someone rewraps. The phrase holds no regex metacharacter, so passing
# it to awk as a pattern matches it literally; one added later would
# quietly turn this into something else.
STANDARD='actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly'
# Three steps state it and one section defines it. Stating it a fifth
# time on purpose means changing this number on purpose.
STANDARDS=4
# Awk's status and its output are both checked, because either can lie
# on its own. A non-number means it did not run -- unsupported construct,
# missing binary, anything -- and compared directly against STANDARDS
# that is a silent pass rather than a failure: the test errors "Illegal
# number", `if` reads the non-zero status as false, and the script goes
# on to print "instructions OK". A number from a command that then
# failed is the same hole from the other side: a shadowed awk printing
# "4" and exiting 17 satisfied the number check, and did it on a file
# whose step 8 had been reworded back to the old standard -- green,
# with the defect present and the counter never having run.
if ! standards=$(awk -v want="$STANDARD" '
	{ s = s " " $0 }
	END { gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s); print gsub(want, "&", s) }' "$AGENTS"); then
	fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run whatever it printed"
else
	case "$standards" in
	'' | *[!0-9]*)
		fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$standards' instead of a number, so this check did not run"
		;;
	*)
		if [ "$standards" -ne "$STANDARDS" ]; then
			fail "AGENTS.md states the finding standard $standards times, expected $STANDARDS -- steps 6, 7 and 8 each state it and 'Answering a finding' defines it. A step reworded on its own no longer visibly agrees with the others; if you added a statement of it on purpose, update STANDARDS in this script"
		fi
		;;
	esac
fi
SECTION='Answering a finding'
# Prefix-matched, so a heading renamed to "### Answering a finding here"
# satisfies this while every pointer names a heading that is gone. That
# is issue #105, and the pointer check below matches the same way:
# awk's index() is literal rather than a BRE, which is a different
# property, but it is still a substring search and a longer heading
# satisfies it too. Fixing one without the other fixes nothing.
if ! grep -q "^### $SECTION" "$AGENTS"; then
	fail "AGENTS.md has no '### $SECTION' section -- step 6 points at it by name, and it is where the standard the three steps state is defined"
# The pointer check is the `else` because it needs the heading to
# locate: with no heading it reports that nothing points forward, which
# is true but reads as a second, separate defect when the pointer is
# sitting there untouched.
else
	# And the pointer to it, which is the one thing tying the numbered steps
	# to the definition. Delete just that clause and the count above still
	# reads 4 and the heading is still there: the section goes on existing
	# with nothing sending a reader to it, which loses the half of #97 that
	# asked where a disagreement is recorded. Matched in quotes because the
	# heading itself is unquoted, so this finds the reference and not the
	# thing referred to.
	#
	# Before the heading, specifically. A mention below it is a
	# back-reference and cannot send anyone anywhere: the reader is
	# already there. Counting mentions instead would pass on a file where
	# step 6's pointer was deleted and the section itself quoted its own
	# name -- one mention either way -- which is the state this exists to
	# catch. The file has one of each again today, so the case is
	# prospective rather than historical, but it has happened once
	# already: a later section quoting the name is what defeated the
	# count that used to stand here.
	#
	# Flattened first, because the pointer is a quoted phrase in wrapped
	# prose and a rewrap that split it across two lines would fail here
	# while the pointer sat there intact. What it cannot see is which step
	# the pointer is in, or a layout that put the section above the steps.
	if ! points=$(awk -v s="$SECTION" '
		{ all = all " " $0 }
		END {
			gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", all)
			h = index(all, "### " s)
			q = index(all, "\"" s "\"")
			print (q > 0 && h > 0 && q < h) ? "yes" : "no"
		}' "$AGENTS"); then
		fail "could not look for the pointer to \"$SECTION\" in AGENTS.md -- awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run"
	else
		# Answered, not merely exited: an awk that prints nothing and
		# succeeds would otherwise pass this the way one printing a
		# plausible number passed the count above before it was guarded.
		case "$points" in
		yes) ;;
		no)
			fail "nothing in AGENTS.md points forward at \"$SECTION\" -- the section defines the standard steps 6, 7 and 8 state, and nothing above it now sends a reader to it"
			;;
		*)
			fail "could not look for the pointer to \"$SECTION\" in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$points' instead of yes or no, so this check did not run"
			;;
		esac
	fi
fi

# CLAUDE.md points at it and holds nothing else.
if ! grep -q '^@AGENTS\.md[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE"; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has no '@AGENTS.md' import line -- Claude Code would not load the shared rules"
fi
# Blank out the one allowed import and see if any other remains. An
# import works mid-line too, so matching only at the start of a line
# would miss `... see @RULES.md:` -- four lines, small, and a second
# source of truth in every session. Only whole tokens are blanked, or
# `@AGENTS.md.bak` would be read as the allowed import plus nothing --
# and since `.` has to count as part of a token for that, sentence
# punctuation after the import is absorbed too.
if sed -E 's#@AGENTS\.md([.,;:!?]?)([^A-Za-z0-9._/-]|$)#\1\2#g' "$CLAUDE" \
		| grep -q '@[A-Za-z0-9._/-]'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md imports a file other than AGENTS.md -- rules should reach agents through AGENTS.md alone"
fi
if [ "$claudebytes" -gt "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md is $claudebytes bytes, over the $MAXBYTES limit -- rules belong in AGENTS.md, not here"
fi

claudelines=$(grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE")
if [ "$claudelines" -gt "$MAXLINES" ]; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md has $claudelines non-blank lines, expected at most $MAXLINES -- if you added a rule, move it to AGENTS.md; if you reworded the pointer, update MAXLINES in this script"
fi

# Rules arrive as list items or new sections. The pointer needs neither,
# so their presence below the title means content landed in the wrong file.
if tail -n +2 "$CLAUDE" | grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*(#|[-*+][[:space:]]|[0-9]+\.[[:space:]])'; then
	fail "CLAUDE.md contains headings or list items below the title -- move that content to AGENTS.md"
fi

# Claude Code also loads CLAUDE.md files from subdirectories (when working
# under them) and from .claude/. Any of those is a second shared source of
# truth, so only the root pointer may exist. A personal, unshared
# CLAUDE.local.md at the root is deliberately left alone -- .gitignore
# keeps it from becoming a shared one.
#
# Matched case-insensitively: macOS filesystems are case-insensitive by
# default, so a lone claude.md there would load like the real thing.
# The prune list mirrors .gitignore's build trees rather than any
# directory merely starting with "build".
extra=$(find "$ROOT" \( -name .git -o -name build -o -name 'build-*' \) -prune -o \
	-iname 'CLAUDE*.md' \
	! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.md" \
	! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.local.md" \
	-print 2>/dev/null)
if [ -n "$extra" ]; then
	fail "these files also carry instructions; fold them into AGENTS.md:"
	echo "$extra" | sed 's/^/         /' >&2
fi

if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
	printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
	printf 'AGENTS.md is the source of truth for every coding agent; CLAUDE.md only imports it.\n' >&2
	printf 'Put project rules in AGENTS.md and leave CLAUDE.md as the pointer.\n' >&2
	exit 1
fi

printf 'instructions OK (CLAUDE.md %s bytes, AGENTS.md %s bytes)\n' "$claudebytes" "$agentsbytes"

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. It decides that scope for itself, per step 7. This says only that it
should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.
Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.

**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest --output-on-failure` prints nothing on a pass, and `-R <name>`
  scopes it to the test being worked on.
- Pipe the shell tests through `tail`. They are written for a human
  watching them run, and every line of that is context spent.
- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

**The mutation proof in step 4 is worth delegating**, unlike the loop it
belongs to. Copying the tree, breaking the game and confirming the test
catches it is a bounded experiment with a one-line answer, and it costs a
fresh configure and build to reach. A sub-agent can run it — but it has to
report what it broke precisely enough for the main agent to write that
down, since step 4 wants it in the commit and in a comment beside the
assertion.

# AGENTS.md keeps some of its rules in named sections below the numbered
# steps, with the steps pointing forward at them by name. Both halves have
# to hold: a heading nothing points at is unreachable, and a pointer with
# no heading sends a reader nowhere. Checked for each such section by
# name, so adding one means adding a call rather than a second copy of
# this.
#
# $1 heading text, $2 what is lost if the heading goes, $3 what is lost if
# the pointer goes.
#
# Prefix-matched, so a heading renamed to "### Answering a finding here"
# satisfies this while every pointer names a heading that is gone. That
# is issue #105, and the pointer check matches the same way: awk's
# index() is literal rather than a BRE, which is a different property,
# but it is still a substring search and a longer heading satisfies it
# too. Fixing one without the other fixes nothing.
check_section() {
	if ! grep -q "^### $1" "$AGENTS"; then
		# Returning here rather than going on to the pointer: with no
		# heading that check reports that nothing points forward, which
		# is true but reads as a second, separate defect when the
		# pointer is sitting there untouched.
		fail "AGENTS.md has no '### $1' section -- $2"
		return
	fi
	# The pointer is the one thing tying the numbered steps to the
	# section. Delete just that clause and the heading is still there:
	# the section goes on existing with nothing sending a reader to it.
	# For "Answering a finding" that loses the half of #97 that asked
	# where a disagreement is recorded, and the standard count above
	# still reads 4 while it happens. Matched in quotes because the
	# heading itself is unquoted, so this finds the reference and not
	# the thing referred to.
	#
	# Before the heading, specifically. A mention below it is a
	# back-reference and cannot send anyone anywhere: the reader is
	# already there. Counting mentions instead would pass on a file
	# where the step's pointer was deleted and the section itself quoted
	# its own name -- one mention either way -- which is the state this
	# exists to catch. It has happened once already: a later section
	# quoting the name is what defeated the count that used to stand
	# here.
	#
	# Flattened first, because the pointer is a quoted phrase in wrapped
	# prose and a rewrap that split it across two lines would fail here
	# while the pointer sat there intact. What it cannot see is which
	# step the pointer is in, or a layout that put the section above the
	# steps.
	if ! points=$(awk -v s="$1" '
		{ all = all " " $0 }
		END {
			gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", all)
			h = index(all, "### " s)
			q = index(all, "\"" s "\"")
			print (q > 0 && h > 0 && q < h) ? "yes" : "no"
		}' "$AGENTS"); then
		fail "could not look for the pointer to \"$1\" in AGENTS.md -- awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run"
		return
	fi
	# Answered, not merely exited: an awk that prints nothing and
	# succeeds would otherwise pass this the way one printing a
	# plausible number passed the count above before it was guarded.
	case "$points" in
	yes) ;;
	no)
		fail "nothing in AGENTS.md points forward at \"$1\" -- $3"
		;;
	*)
		fail "could not look for the pointer to \"$1\" in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$points' instead of yes or no, so this check did not run"
		;;
	esac
}

`AGENTS.md:40-42` says CI configures with `-DSST_WERROR=ON` and tells the
reader to "pass that locally to see what CI will refuse". The `verifier` is
the pass that stands between a local change and CI, and its definition never
mentions the flag:

```
.claude/agents/verifier.md:19  cmake -S . -B build-debug   -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug   && cmake --build build-debug
.claude/agents/verifier.md:20  cmake -S . -B build-release -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build-release
```

## Why it matters

A warning that CI will reject is invisible to every pass the workflow runs
before CI. The `verifier` reports "zero warnings" from a build that was never
asked to treat them as errors, which reads as the stronger claim.

The gap got sharper with the `### Who runs which tests` section added in
PR #125: that section assigns `-DSST_WERROR=ON` to the `verifier` as one of
"the configurations the main agent did not build". So AGENTS.md now says the
verifier owns it, and `verifier.md` still does not ask for it — on the letter
of the two files, nobody builds it. In practice the sub-agent has been passing
it anyway when told to, which is worse than either: the behaviour depends on
what the invoking prompt happens to say.

## How to see it

Compare `.claude/agents/verifier.md:19-20` against `AGENTS.md:40-42`. Then note
that `AGENTS.md`'s "The review sub-agents" section says a per-tool definition
"should say to read the matching file and follow it, and carry only the wiring
its own harness needs" — the configure lines in `verifier.md` are neither
wiring nor a pointer, they are a restatement that has drifted.

## Fix sketch

Either add `-DSST_WERROR=ON` to both configure lines, or drop the lines and
point at `AGENTS.md`'s "Build and run" section, which already carries the flag
and the reason. The second is what "The review sub-agents" argues for and
cannot drift again.

## Provenance

Found by the `verifier` while verifying PR #125. Filed rather than fixed
there: `verifier.md` is a reviewer definition, and AGENTS.md requires those to
land as their own change, on their own branch and commit, before the work they
review.
EOF

cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/i2.md" <<'EOF'
`check_section()` in `tests/instructions.sh` asks for the section heading and
for **one** quoted mention of the section name somewhere above it. Its failure
message for the new `Who runs which tests` section, however, says:

> steps 4 and 7 point at it

Both really do today (`AGENTS.md:152` and `AGENTS.md:229`). Delete either one
and the test stays green while the message's claim stops being true — verified
both ways by the `verifier`: with only step 4's pointer the script exits 0, and
with only step 7's it exits 0.

## Why it matters

The section is reached from two different steps because they do two different
things with it — step 4 is told not to delegate its loop, step 7 is told the
battery is its own work. Losing either pointer loses that step's reader, and
nothing notices. This is a check that asserts less than its own error message
claims, which is the shape AGENTS.md step 9 asks to be filed.

The same is true of `Answering a finding`, which steps 6, 7 and 8 all state and
which one surviving mention satisfies. It is only sharper for the new section
because its message names the two steps.

## How to see it

```sh
python3 - <<'PY'
import re
t = open('AGENTS.md').read()
open('/tmp/a/AGENTS.md','w').write(re.sub(r'"Who runs which\s+tests" after this list says why', 'it says why', t))
PY
cp CLAUDE.md /tmp/a/ && sh tests/instructions.sh /tmp/a    # exits 0, step 4's pointer gone
```

Note the newline-aware replacement: step 4's pointer wraps mid-phrase, so a
line-wise `sed` cannot remove it. `tests/instructions.sh` carries a comment
about that, since it is how the first mutation attempt against this check came
back green for the wrong reason.

## Fix sketch

Counting pointers rather than finding one would catch it, at the cost of a
number to maintain per section — the same trade `STANDARDS` already makes a few
lines above, and with the same failure mode when someone rewords legitimately.
The stronger fix is the one #65 and #105 are circling: attribute a pointer to
the step it sits in, so the check can say "step 4 no longer points at this"
rather than "nothing does". None of the three can be done well without that
attribution, so this may belong to #65 rather than to a fix of its own.

## Provenance

Reported by the `verifier` as missing coverage while verifying the change that
added the section. Filed rather than fixed there, per AGENTS.md step 9.
EOF
gh issue create --title "instructions.sh accepts one pointer where its message claims two" --body-file "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/i2.md"

cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/i4.md" <<'EOF'
`tests/tui.sh:91-94` sets four traps:

```sh
trap 'finish' EXIT
trap 'finish; exit 130' INT
trap 'finish; exit 143' TERM
trap 'finish; exit 129' HUP
```

The other three shell tests that dump on failure all set a fifth:

```
tests/help.sh:42        trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE
tests/golden.sh:73      trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE
tests/tournament.sh:103 trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 141' PIPE
```

`tui.sh` is the one without it, and it is the one with the most to clean up.

## What happens

Pipe it into anything that can exit early — `head`, `grep -q`, `less` and a
`q` — and the script takes SIGPIPE, dies, and its `EXIT` trap never runs.
`finish` is what kills the private tmux server, so what is left behind is:

- a `tmux -f /dev/null -L sst-tui-<pid>` server, still running
- the `sst -t` process inside it, still running
- the socket under `/tmp/tmux-1000/`
- the `/tmp/sst-tui.XXXXXX` working directory

Reproduced by the `verifier` with both `head -3` and a bare `head`. A single
pane dump is about 26 lines, so `head`'s 10-line default is exceeded by the
first failing assertion — this needs no unusual invocation, only a failing run
that someone pipes.

## It has already happened

Two orphans are sitting on this machine right now, from before the branch that
found this:

```
/tmp/sst-tui.474IVX   Aug 10 19:27
/tmp/sst-tui.6Q7RWJ   Aug  8 20:43
```

with matching tmux servers still alive. Nobody noticed, which is the point:
the leak is silent, and the server has a per-run name nobody would think to
look for.

## Why it matters beyond the litter

`AGENTS.md` tells every agent to keep test output out of its context, and the
obvious way to do that is a pipe. So the advice most likely to be followed is
the one that trips this. The `### Who runs which tests` section added on
`docs/agents-test-split` now has to tell readers to redirect to a file rather
than pipe, and cite this issue for why — which is a workaround in an
instruction file standing in for a one-line fix in a test.

## Fix sketch

```sh
trap 'finish; exit 141' PIPE
```

matching the other three scripts. Worth checking at the same time whether
`finish` is safe to run when a write to stdout is what failed — it calls
`tmux kill-server` on its own socket, which does not write to stdout, so it
should be.

The `verifier` also noted the general shape: nothing checks that these four
scripts agree on their trap sets. That is a second, smaller issue if anyone
wants it.

Found by the `verifier` while verifying the `docs/agents-test-split` branch,
when the branch's own advice to pipe test output was measured. Filed rather
than fixed there, per AGENTS.md step 9 — it is a defect the change did not
cause. The two orphaned servers above were left alone; they are not this
session's, and `AGENTS.md` forbids a bare `tmux kill-server`.

### Who runs which tests

Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
`verifier` runs everything else.** The line does not fall between unit
tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about. A change to the
pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs in the loop, slow
as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled `tuifmt` test the
focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest to the `verifier`
— including
the golden recordings, which never pass `-t` and so cannot see that file's
panel formatters at all, whatever else in it they reach.

Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all. It asks you to watch a test fail
for the expected reason, and a sub-agent reporting that it failed correctly
is exactly the trust that failing run exists to withhold. It is also the
tightest loop in the workflow, where a sub-agent round trip costs minutes
against a `ctest -R` that costs a second.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. It decides that scope for itself: step 7 gives it the criterion, and
step 8 says the decision is the verifier's own. This says only that it
should not be asked to skip what the main agent happened to run, and that
the main agent should not pre-run the battery to save it the trouble.
Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
`ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.

**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest --output-on-failure` prints no test output on a pass, and `-R`
  scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern, since it is a
  regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On
  a failure they print what broke and then dump the screen behind it, in

### Who runs which tests

Steps 4 and 7 both run tests, and they are not running the same ones.

**The main agent runs the test that is the subject of the change. The
`verifier` runs the rest of the battery.** Not everything else: the piped
plain-mode journey above and the 80x24/72x24 TUI check stay with whoever
made the change, since they are how you see your own work. The line does not
fall between unit tests and journeys; it falls on what the change is about.
A change to the pager makes `tests/tui.sh` the focused test and it belongs
in the loop, slow as it is. A change to `tuifmt.c` makes the compiled
`tuifmt` test the focused one, fast as it is, and leaves `tui` and the rest
to the `verifier` — including the golden recordings, which never pass `-t`
and so cannot see that file's panel formatters at all, whatever else in it
they reach.



Step 4's loop cannot be delegated at all, and not because a sub-agent
cannot be trusted with it. Each failure decides the next edit, so the run
and the work are one act: what you would hand over is the whole of the
task, and a report arriving afterwards comes after the moment it was
supposed to inform. It is also the tightest loop in the workflow, where a
sub-agent round trip costs minutes against a `ctest -R` that costs a
second.

What the `verifier` owns is everything the loop did not reach: the rest of
`ctest`, the full journey and golden battery, and the configurations the
main agent did not build — Release, `-DSST_WERROR=ON`, whatever the platform
adds. `verifier.md` does not yet ask for that flag, which is #125; until it
does, say so when invoking the pass. It decides that scope for itself: step
7 gives it the criterion, and step 8 says the decision is the verifier's
own. This says only that it should not be asked to skip what the main agent
happened to run, and that the main agent should not pre-run the battery to
save it the trouble. Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the
whole of it: a full `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.



**Keep what reaches the main agent's context small.** That is the reason
this split is worth stating, and it is mechanical:

- `ctest` prints no test output on a pass at all, and `--output-on-failure`
  costs nothing there while saving the second run a failure would otherwise
  need. `-R` scopes it to the test being worked on — anchor the pattern,
  since it is a regex: `-R tui` picks up `tuifmt` and `journey-tui` with it.
- The shell tests print one line on a pass, so they need no filtering. On a
  failure they print what broke and then dump the evidence behind it — a
  pane, a slice of game output, a diff, depending on the script — in that
  order, so it is the first lines that are worth reading and not the last.
  Redirect to a file and read the head of that rather than piping:
  `tests/tui.sh` has no `PIPE` trap, so a `head` that closes the pipe early
  leaves it holding a live tmux server and an `sst -t` inside it (#128).
- Grep a tmux pane for the string being asserted rather than capturing it
  whole. `capture-pane -p` is twenty-odd lines of screen and a TUI check
  makes many; capture the pane when the grep fails, which is when its
  content is worth reading.

**The mutation proof in step 4 can be delegated**, unlike the loop it
belongs to, and for the reason the loop cannot: it is one shot, asked and
answered, and what comes back is checkable. The break has a name, and step
4 wants that name written down anyway, so a report that does not give it is
visibly incomplete.

Not to one of the three review sub-agents — all of them are read-only by
definition, and this one has to break the game. A general-purpose sub-agent
does it, on a copy outside the repository, which step 4 requires in any
case: no file in the repository is modified.

What handing it off buys is context and not time. Nothing here comes near a
sub-agent round trip even when it fails, and a failing run is what a proof
is: a broken `tui.sh` goes past two minutes, its failed polls waiting out
their timeouts on top of a run that is slow already, where a round trip is
several. Delegate when the failing run would bury this context instead,
which is a property of the test and worth looking up rather than guessing —
one ordinary break in `tui.sh` printed nineteen panes and four hundred lines
of them, `tournament.sh` dumps up to 3000 bytes for every seed that fails,
`golden.sh` a diff per changed journey. Below that, and most proofs are
below it — a `ctest -R '^tuifmt$'` answering in a second, a `help` journey
in eight — running it costs less than handing it over.



When you do hand it off, the sub-agent has to report what it broke precisely
enough for the main agent to write that down, since step 4 wants it in the
commit and in a comment beside the assertion.

### The review sub-agents

cat > "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/i5.md" <<'EOF'
`check_section()` in `tests/instructions.sh` locates a section heading with:

```sh
grep -q "^### $1" "$AGENTS"
```

`$1` is interpolated into a basic regular expression. The pointer half of the
same function passes `$1` to `awk -v` and searches with `index()`, which is
literal. The comment above the function notes that the two "match the same
way" as a substring search and calls the difference "a different property",
but never says that one side is a regex and the other is not.

## Why it matters

Neither section name has a metacharacter today, so nothing is wrong now:

```
check_section 'Answering a finding' ...
check_section 'Who runs which tests' ...
```

The function is the documented extension point — its own comment says "adding
one means adding a call rather than a second copy of this" — so the next name
is written by someone following that instruction, and nothing warns them. A
heading like `### The 3.x flags` or `### Answering a finding (and when not to)`
matches a different set of lines through `grep` than through `index()`, and the
two halves of the check would then disagree about whether the section exists.
Backslashes are worse: `grep` consumes them and `awk -v` consumes them again.

The failure is silent in the direction that matters — a heading check that
matches too loosely passes, which is the same shape as #105.

## How to see it

```sh
sed -i 's/^### Answering a finding$/### Answering a finding./' AGENTS.md
sh tests/instructions.sh .        # passes: `.` matches the real heading's own text
```

## Fix sketch

Match the heading literally on both sides — `grep -qF -- "### $1"` loses the
line anchor, so either `awk 'index($0, "### " s) == 1'` for both halves, or
keep `grep` and escape the name. Whichever, the two halves should use the same
matching rule, since the comment already claims they do.

Worth doing together with #105 and #126: all three are about this check being
looser than it reads, and a rewrite that gives it per-step attribution would
be the moment to make the matching literal as well.

## Provenance

Reported by the `verifier` while verifying the `docs/agents-test-split` branch,
which generalized the hard-coded check into `check_section()` and so turned a
latent property of one call into an extension point. Filed rather than fixed
there, per AGENTS.md step 9.
EOF
gh issue create --title "check_section() matches headings as a regex on one side and literally on the other" --body-file "$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp/i5.md"

the tree you are working in is a surprise nobody needs.
